lessonTitle: Mechanisms of Drug Interactions: Enzyme Induction, Inhibition and Pharmacodynamic Interaction

blocks.text: A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive starts a herbal remedy for low mood and, within weeks, develops breakthrough bleeding. The herbal product, St John's wort, has switched on liver enzymes that destroy contraceptive hormones faster than usual. Many drug interactions are not rare accidents but predictable consequences of a few mechanisms.

blocks.markdown: A **drug interaction** occurs when one drug alters the effect of another. Interactions are classified as **pharmacokinetic** (one drug changes the absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of another, altering its concentration) or **pharmacodynamic** (the drugs act at the same or related targets or physiological systems and their effects add, oppose or synergise, without any change in concentration). The commonest and most important pharmacokinetic mechanisms involve the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes.

blocks.title: Enzyme inducers and inhibitors
blocks.text: An enzyme inducer increases the synthesis of metabolising enzymes (CYPs), so substrate drugs are cleared faster and their levels fall. An enzyme inhibitor reduces enzyme activity (often competitively and within hours to days), so substrate drugs are cleared more slowly and their levels rise. A substrate is the drug whose metabolism is altered.

blocks.caption: Examples of enzyme inducers and inhibitors and their effect on substrates.
rows: Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort, chronic heavy alcohol
Loss of effect, for example oral contraceptive failure or reduced warfarin effect
Clarithromycin and erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole and other azoles, ritonavir, grapefruit juice, omeprazole (for CYP2C19), amiodarone
Toxicity, for example raised INR with warfarin
Alcohol plus benzodiazepine; ACE inhibitor plus potassium-sparing diuretic; aspirin plus warfarin
No change in drug level; combined effects

blocks.caption: At steady state, concentration is inversely proportional to clearance. An inhibitor lowers CL, so Css rises; an inducer raises CL, so Css falls, if dose and bioavailability are unchanged.

blocks.title: Effect of an inducer on a drug with a stable dose
blocks.prompt: A patient takes carbamazepine and warfarin. Carbamazepine increases warfarin clearance by 50% (to 1.5 times its original value). The warfarin dose is unchanged. What happens to the steady-state effect, and what happens when carbamazepine is later stopped? (Qualitative teaching example.)

steps.text: Apply Css = dose rate x F / CL. With clearance 1.5 times larger and the same dose, Css falls to 1 / 1.5 = 0.67 of its previous value.

A fall of about one-third in warfarin concentration lowers the anticoagulant effect, so the INR falls below target and thrombotic risk rises. The prescriber raises the warfarin dose under INR monitoring.
Induction takes days to weeks to develop (new enzyme must be synthesised) and equally long to wear off.

When carbamazepine is stopped, enzyme levels gradually return to normal, clearance of warfarin falls back, and the now-raised warfarin dose gives too high an INR with a bleeding risk. The dose must be reduced with close monitoring.

blocks.answer: Warfarin level and INR fall during induction (raise the dose); stopping the inducer causes the INR to rise (reduce the dose).

blocks.markdown: **Warfarin and a macrolide.** Warfarin is a racemic mixture whose enantiomers are metabolised by several CYP enzymes (including CYP2C9, CYP3A4 and CYP1A2). Macrolides such as erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP enzymes, so warfarin clearance falls and its plasma concentration rises. A stable patient may then experience a marked rise in the INR and increased risk of bleeding. The effect usually develops over several days of co-prescription. The interaction is predictable, so the INR should be checked within a few days of starting or stopping the antibiotic, or a non-interacting antibiotic should be chosen.

blocks.title: Time course
blocks.text: Inhibition begins as soon as the inhibitor reaches adequate concentration (hours to a few days) and wears off as it is eliminated. Induction is slower, taking days to weeks to develop and to disappear, because it needs synthesis or degradation of enzyme protein.

blocks.markdown: **Pharmacodynamic interactions** occur at the level of effect. They may be **additive or synergistic** (two sedatives, two QT-prolonging drugs, an anticoagulant plus an antiplatelet drug) or **antagonistic** (a beta-agonist reliever plus a beta-blocker). No change in plasma concentration is needed. Other pharmacokinetic mechanisms include altered absorption (for example tetracyclines chelated by calcium or iron), displacement from plasma protein binding, and altered renal excretion (for example NSAIDs reducing lithium clearance).

blocks.title: Classifying and predicting an interaction
blocks.prompt: A patient's drug has Css = 8 mg/L. An inhibitor halves its clearance. Predict the new Css and classify the interaction. A second patient takes two sedatives and becomes drowsy with no change in either drug level. Classify that interaction. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: For the first patient, Css = dose rate x F / CL. Halving CL doubles Css: 8 x 2 = 16 mg/L.
Because the concentration changed through altered metabolism, this is a pharmacokinetic (metabolic inhibition) interaction.
For the second patient, plasma concentrations are unchanged but the combined effect is increased. Both drugs depress the central nervous system, so the effects add: a pharmacodynamic interaction.
Management differs: for the first, reduce the dose or avoid the inhibitor and monitor levels; for the second, avoid the combination or use lower doses with monitoring of sedation.

blocks.answer: Css rises to 16 mg/L (pharmacokinetic); the sedative pair is pharmacodynamic.

items: Pharmacokinetic interactions change drug concentration; pharmacodynamic interactions change response at a given concentration.
Narrow therapeutic index drugs (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, ciclosporin) are most at risk of clinically important interactions.
Always check for interactions, including herbal and over-the-counter products, when starting or stopping any drug.
When an inducer or inhibitor is stopped, remember the reverse effect.

blocks.title: Do not forget the offset
blocks.text: Interactions can emerge when a drug is stopped. Stopping an inducer lets a previously raised dose of the substrate become an overdose over the next weeks.

points: Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) lower substrate levels; inhibitors (macrolides, azoles, grapefruit juice) raise them.
Warfarin with a macrolide: CYP inhibition reduces warfarin clearance, raising the INR and bleeding risk, so monitor or avoid.
Pharmacokinetic interactions change drug concentration, whereas pharmacodynamic interactions change the combined effect at the same concentration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognised cytochrome P450 enzyme inducer?

options.text: Rifampicin
Clarithromycin
Ketoconazole
Grapefruit juice

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 and other enzymes.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4.

questions.explanation: Rifampicin increases transcription of CYP enzymes, accelerating metabolism of substrates such as oral contraceptives and warfarin. The other options inhibit metabolism and so raise substrate levels.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman on a combined oral contraceptive is started on rifampicin for tuberculosis. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: Faster metabolism of contraceptive hormones, reducing contraceptive efficacy
Slower metabolism of contraceptive hormones, causing toxicity
Renal retention of contraceptive hormones
No effect, since the drugs act on different organs

questions.correctOptionText: Faster metabolism of contraceptive hormones, reducing contraceptive efficacy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: induction of CYP3A4 lowers hormone levels and can cause contraceptive failure.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this would result from an inhibitor.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: the interaction is metabolic, not renal.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: pharmacokinetic interactions do not depend on shared target organs.

questions.explanation: Rifampicin induces hepatic CYP enzymes, so ethinylestradiol and progestogen are cleared faster and their levels fall. Alternative contraception is therefore needed during and for a period after rifampicin.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on stable warfarin (INR 2.5) is prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection. Five days later his INR is 6.8 and he has bruising. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Inhibition of CYP enzymes reduces warfarin clearance and raises its concentration
Induction of CYP enzymes increases warfarin clearance
Clarithromycin displaces vitamin K from binding sites
Clarithromycin increases warfarin excretion by the kidney

questions.correctOptionText: Inhibition of CYP enzymes reduces warfarin clearance and raises its concentration

distractorRationale.a: Correct: macrolides inhibit CYP-mediated warfarin metabolism.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: induction would lower the INR.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: this is not the mechanism and vitamin K is not displaced.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: warfarin is cleared by metabolism, not renal excretion.

questions.explanation: Clarithromycin inhibits the CYP enzymes that metabolise warfarin, so its clearance falls and the anticoagulant effect rises, causing a high INR and bleeding risk. Warfarin dose reduction or antibiotic substitution with close INR monitoring is required.

questions.stem: A patient has a steady-state plasma concentration of 12 mg/L on a fixed dose. A new enzyme inhibitor reduces the drug's clearance to 40% of its original value (0.4 times), with the dose and bioavailability unchanged. Calculate the new steady-state concentration in mg/L.
questions.explanation: Css is inversely proportional to clearance, so Css(new) = 12 / 0.4 = 30 mg/L. A 60% fall in clearance produces a 2.5-fold rise in level.

questions.stem: A drug has a steady-state concentration of 10 mg/L on a fixed dose. After an enzyme inducer is started, the clearance becomes 2.5 times higher with dose and bioavailability unchanged. Calculate the new steady-state concentration in mg/L.
questions.explanation: Css = dose rate x F / CL, so a 2.5-fold rise in CL divides Css by 2.5: 10 / 2.5 = 4 mg/L. The level may fall below the effective range.

questions.stem: A patient on an ACE inhibitor is started on spironolactone and later develops serum potassium of 6.4 mmol/L. How is this interaction best classified?

options.text: Pharmacodynamic, because both drugs reduce renal potassium excretion
Pharmacokinetic, because the ACE inhibitor inhibits CYP3A4
Pharmacokinetic, because of altered absorption
Not an interaction, since the drugs are in different classes

questions.correctOptionText: Pharmacodynamic, because both drugs reduce renal potassium excretion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: additive effects on potassium handling without a change in either drug's level.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: ACE inhibitors do not inhibit CYP3A4.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: drugs in different classes can still interact.

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and spironolactone blocks its receptor, so their effects on potassium add together. No change in drug concentration is needed, so the interaction is pharmacodynamic.

questions.stem: True or false: the effect of an enzyme inducer reaches its maximum within a few hours of the first dose.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Induction requires increased synthesis of enzyme protein and so develops over days to weeks. Inhibition, by contrast, can begin within hours once adequate inhibitor concentrations are reached.

questions.stem: Distinguish pharmacokinetic from pharmacodynamic drug interactions, giving an example of each and naming the four pharmacokinetic processes that may be affected.
markingGuide: Pharmacokinetic: one drug alters absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of another, changing its concentration
Pharmacodynamic: effects add or oppose at the same or related targets without altering concentration
Example PK: rifampicin induction lowering oral contraceptive levels, or clarithromycin inhibiting warfarin metabolism, or chelation of tetracycline by calcium
Example PD: benzodiazepine plus alcohol sedation, ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone hyperkalaemia, warfarin plus aspirin bleeding
Clinical implication: PK interactions can be addressed by dose adjustment guided by levels or monitoring; PD by avoiding or monitoring the combination
questions.explanation: The distinguishing question is whether drug concentration changes (pharmacokinetic) or whether the response at a given concentration changes (pharmacodynamic). This guides how the interaction is detected and managed.

questions.stem: Explain the interaction between warfarin and a macrolide antibiotic such as erythromycin, and outline how the risk should be managed.
markingGuide: Warfarin is cleared largely by hepatic CYP metabolism
Macrolides inhibit CYP enzymes so warfarin clearance falls and concentration rises
Higher warfarin effect raises the INR and the risk of bleeding
Develops over days; narrow therapeutic index magnifies the effect
Management: choose a non-interacting antibiotic if possible, otherwise check INR within a few days, adjust warfarin dose, and check again when the antibiotic stops
questions.explanation: Macrolide inhibition lowers warfarin clearance, so at an unchanged dose the steady-state level and INR rise. Because warfarin's therapeutic index is narrow, close INR monitoring is essential.

questions.stem: Which statement about drug interactions after stopping an enzyme inducer such as carbamazepine is correct?

options.text: Enzyme levels fall over weeks, so substrate levels rise and doses previously raised may need to be reduced
Substrate levels fall immediately after the inducer is stopped
No further adjustment is ever needed
The inducer interaction was pharmacodynamic and disappears at once

questions.correctOptionText: Enzyme levels fall over weeks, so substrate levels rise and doses previously raised may need to be reduced

distractorRationale.a: Correct: offset of induction is gradual, and an inflated substrate dose becomes excessive as enzymes return to baseline.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: levels rise, not fall, when induction wears off.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: induction is a pharmacokinetic interaction and wears off slowly.

questions.explanation: Induced enzyme protein declines slowly, so clearance gradually returns to baseline. Doses of substrates that were raised to compensate for induction will then produce higher levels and toxicity unless reduced.
